Reproducibility: not applicable. This PR requests a new design and support-boundary decision rather than reporting broken current behavior.

target.title: RFC: Standard Hosting Profiles and Ready Check
target.body:
## Decision requested

Should OpenClaw own a small set of named, release-tested hosting contracts and report whether the running process currently satisfies the selected contract?

This RFC extends surfaces OpenClaw already owns: Gateway `/ready` and `/readyz`, health, and status. It does **not** add a second config system, a general policy engine, or a hosted-platform abstraction.

## The concrete gap

OpenClaw can run in containers today, but “the process is alive” is not the same as “this runtime shape is usable.”

A container can start with a loopback-only Gateway. Existing lifecycle readiness may correctly say the process is healthy while the selected container topology is unreachable. Hosts currently fill that gap with private startup scripts, baked config checks, and downstream-only readiness logic.

Profiles make the support promise executable:

```text
OpenClaw supports these runtime shapes.
Each shape has stable predicates and failure reasons.
Each release validates them.
A running instance reports which shape it selected and whether it satisfies it.
```

## Binary readiness without losing diagnostics

Each condition carries:

```text
type + status + requirement + reason + message
```

`requirement` is either:

| Class | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `required` | `False` or `Unknown` blocks readiness and appears in `failures` |
| `advisory` | `False` or `Unknown` appears in `advisories` but does not change 200 to 503 |

Existing Gateway lifecycle failures are also merged into `failures`. The binary result remains suitable for Docker/Kubernetes while health/status retain useful degraded-state diagnostics.

## Narrow design

| Invariant | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| Profiles use existing config and runtime facts | No parallel hosted config tree |
| Profiles never generate, merge, or repair config | Operators retain normal OpenClaw configuration |
| Profile readiness is ANDed with existing Gateway readiness | Startup, channel, drain, and event-loop checks remain authoritative |
| Only required conditions affect binary readiness | Useful diagnostics do not automatically become outages |
| Core owns only built-in predicates | No dependency on policy, doctor, OCC, Lobster, or optional plugins |
| Host timing stays in the host | Docker/Kubernetes/systemd own retries, intervals, and start periods |

Selection is deterministic:

```text
gateway startup flag > environment > openclaw.json > local default
```

Invalid explicit values fail instead of silently selecting a different profile.

## Proposed built-in contracts

| Profile | Required additional assertion | Advisory |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `local` | config loaded and Gateway observed | selected plugin activation health |
| `container` | Gateway is local and the resolved listener is non-loopback | inherited plugin health |
| `reverse-proxy` | trusted-proxy auth has a user header and trusted source | inherited plugin health |
| `managed` | managed ingress uses the trusted-proxy contract; existing Gateway readiness owns lifecycle | inherited plugin health |
| `node-mode` | an approved node is live, correlated, controllable, and advertises an allowed command | inherited plugin health |

The RFC deliberately does not add custom profiles or custom evidence publication. That requires a separate trust, identity, scoping, and freshness contract.

## Why core instead of doctor or policy?

Doctor can diagnose or repair static configuration. Policy can restrict allowed configuration. Both are optional.

A supervisor consumes readiness during startup and continuously afterward. Core owns the authoritative live Gateway, plugin, proxy, pairing, and node-registry facts. Doctor and policy can consume the result later without becoming startup dependencies.

## Compatibility and stability

No profile selection is required; `local` is the default, and selection never changes runtime configuration.

Plugin activation errors are advisory in `local`. They become visible through stable conditions without changing an existing healthy probe from 200 to 503.

Condition identity and requirement class are part of the support contract. Turning an advisory into required, adding a required condition, or changing a stable reason requires compatibility review, release notes, and conformance coverage.

## Smallest useful landing

1. Canonical condition shape plus default `local` projection on existing readiness/health/status.
2. Explicit selection plus container/reverse-proxy/managed predicates.
3. Node-mode predicates from pairing and the live node registry.

The first slice is independently useful. Accepting the readiness foundation does not require committing to every proposed profile immediately.

## Concrete draft stack

| Slice | Draft fork PR |
| --- | --- |
| Local readiness surfaces | https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/17 (`bf44ae3b45`) |
| Built-in profile selection and predicates | https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/18 (`cc43cc5a02`) |
| Node-mode readiness | https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/19 (`88d44534af`) |

Each slice was tested and reviewed against its actual base. Docker behavior proof remains before opening upstream implementation PRs.

## OCC and hosting platforms

OCC can select a profile as declarative desired state. OpenClaw evaluates it in the runtime plane. OCC does not enter channel, session, tool, approval, or AgentHarness traffic.

Lobster and other hosts remain responsible for auth integration, tenant routing, policy rollout, telemetry, administration, and deployment. OpenClaw owns only the generic workload contract those hosts should not reimplement.
